blocks.text: Every conversation you have with an AI assistant runs on context, the facts, documents and data the model is actually looking at when it answers you. MCP resources are the mechanism a server uses to hand that context over.

" This lesson is about understanding resources as a concept before you touch a single line of the protocol that implements them, because the concept is genuinely simple, and getting it solid now makes everything later in this module click faster.
1. The Core Idea: Context You Can Read

blocks.alt: A resource is context that a model can read
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737275-46435192.png

A resource is a readable piece of context that an MCP server makes available to a client. Think of it as a labeled, addressable chunk of information sitting on the server side that a client can ask for and receive back, usually as text or as raw bytes.

A resource does not run any code when you access it beyond whatever is needed to fetch or generate its content, it does not change anything, it does not send an email, it does not write to a database. It just hands over what it already represents.

This sounds almost too simple to need its own name, and in a sense that is exactly the point. MCP intentionally keeps the concept narrow so that a client, and the human or model behind it, always knows what kind of thing it is dealing with. If something is described as a resource, you already know, before reading a single word of its documentation, that fetching it is safe and side effect free.

It is also worth noticing what a resource is not. It is not a function you call with arguments, it is not a stream you subscribe to by default, and it is not a promise of future computation. It is closer to a named, addressable snapshot of something, fetched fresh each time you ask, but conceptually simple in a way that keeps clients from needing to guess at hidden behavior.
2. Read vs Do: The Distinction That Defines Everything

blocks.alt: A resource is read only while a tool performs an action
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737275-356550348.png

MCP splits what a server can offer into two very different buckets. Resources are things a client can read. Tools are things a client can invoke to make something happen. A file on disk is a resource. Sending that file as an email attachment is a tool call. A row in a database is a resource. Deleting that row is a tool call. The line is not about how complicated the underlying operation is, it is about whether the operation observes the world or changes it.

Keeping this distinction sharp is what lets a host application reason about risk. Listing and reading resources can happen automatically, quietly, in the background, without asking a human for permission, because nothing is at stake. Invoking a tool is a different story, and many host applications insert a confirmation step before a tool call is allowed to run precisely because tools can have real, lasting effects.

blocks.text: It can help to notice that this split mirrors a distinction good API designers have used for decades, separating idempotent, side effect free reads from mutating writes. MCP did not invent the idea that reading and doing deserve different treatment, it simply gives that old idea a first class place in the protocol, so every client and every server author inherits the same vocabulary for it instead of reinventing their own convention each time.
3. Resources Are Passive by Design

It helps to picture a resource less like a function and more like a library book. You can walk in, find the book by its call number, and read it. Reading it does not rearrange the shelves, does not check the book out on someone else's card, does not change what the book says for the next person. The library, in MCP terms the server, might have generated that book on demand the moment you asked, but from your side as the reader, the act of reading was purely observational.

This passivity is a promise the protocol makes on behalf of the server. A well behaved MCP server never treats a resources/read call as a place to smuggle in a side effect, no incrementing counters that matter, no triggering downstream jobs, no mutating anything a user would care about. If an operation has a side effect worth naming, it belongs modeled as a tool instead, even if fetching some data is also involved along the way.

This does not mean a resource's content has to be static or precomputed. A resource can absolutely be assembled at the moment it is requested, running a live query, checking a live sensor, calling out to another system. What matters is the direction of the effect: information flows from the world into the response, never the other way around as a result of the read itself.
4. How the Model Actually Sees a Resource

When a host application decides to include a resource in a conversation, it fetches that resource's content and inserts it into the context window the model sees, typically as plain text sitting alongside the user's message and the conversation history. From the model's point of view, a resource that has been read looks exactly like any other piece of text it is reasoning over, there is no special resource-shaped hole in the model's attention, the content is simply there.

Notice the resource's content sits right there in the message, already fetched, already resolved. Nothing about the model's prompt construction needs to know MCP exists, the host did the work of turning a resource reference into inline content before the model ever saw the request.

This also explains why resources are so composable with ordinary prompting. Since a fetched resource ultimately becomes plain text or structured content sitting in a message, everything you already know about writing clear prompts still applies, the resource is simply additional, grounded material the model reasons over alongside the user's own words.
5. Files as Resources

blocks.alt: Files, database records, documents, and config all count as resources
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737276-856716460.png

The most intuitive example of a resource is a file on disk. A file system MCP server might expose every file under a project directory as a resource, each one addressed by a file:// URI. A client browsing a codebase, answering a question about a particular module, or summarizing a log file is really just reading resources one at a time.

A file system server does not need to expose every single file on disk either. Most implementations scope resources to a specific project directory or an explicitly allowed set of paths, both for practical reasons, nobody wants a resource list with millions of entries, and for security reasons covered in depth in the resource security lesson later in this module.
6. Database Records as Resources

A resource does not have to correspond to a physical file. A server sitting in front of a database might expose individual rows, or the results of a saved query, as resources, each addressed by a custom URI scheme the server invents itself. The client never needs to know or care that behind the scenes this URI turns into a SQL query, all it sees is a readable, addressable piece of data.

This pattern generalizes well beyond a single row. A server might expose an entire saved query's results as one resource, or expose a whole table's schema as a resource distinct from any individual row. The common thread is always the same, a URI that names something readable, and content that reflects the current state of that thing at the moment it was read.
7. Documents and Knowledge Bases as Resources
Wikis, support articles, internal runbooks and knowledge base entries are natural resources too.

A documentation server might expose each article by its slug or internal identifier, letting a client pull in exactly the article relevant to a question rather than dumping an entire knowledge base into context at once.

This is one of the most common real world uses of resources, since it lets an assistant answer questions grounded in a company's actual, current documentation rather than whatever the model happened to memorize during training.

This is also where resources and retrieval overlap in practice. A search-backed knowledge base might not know every article it could return ahead of time, in which case the individual articles behave more like the dynamic resources covered two lessons from now, generated in response to a query rather than existing as a fixed, enumerable set.
8. Configuration and Settings as Resources

Configuration files, environment descriptions, feature flag states and deployment manifests are resources any operations focused MCP server is likely to expose. These are exactly the kind of thing a human engineer would read, never edit through casual conversation, before diagnosing a problem, which makes them a natural fit for the read only nature of a resource.

One nuance worth flagging early, exposing configuration as a resource is very different from exposing secrets as one. A well designed server redacts credentials, API keys and tokens before ever handing configuration back as a resource, since a resource's content is exactly the kind of thing that might end up inside a model's context, and eventually inside a conversation transcript.
9. Every Resource Has an Identity

blocks.alt: A resource has a URI that gives it a stable identity
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737276-597085607.png
A resource is always addressed by a URI, a single string that uniquely identifies it within the server's namespace.

This is what makes a resource a stable, referenceable thing rather than a one-off blob of text, a client can hold onto a URI, pass it around, log it, and come back to fetch the same resource again later.
The mechanics of URIs get their own full lesson right after this one, but the important idea here is simply that identity is not optional, every resource has exactly one.

Because the URI is stable, it also becomes something a client can safely cache, log, or store for later, referring back to the exact same resource across an entire session, or even across sessions, without needing to re-discover it through a fresh resources/list call every time.
10. Resources Carry Metadata, Not Just Content

Alongside its URI, a resource typically carries a human readable name, an optional description, and a MIME type telling the client what kind of content to expect before it even fetches anything. This metadata is what powers resource discovery, letting a client show a sensible list of what is available without needing to read every single resource up front just to figure out what it is.

The mimeType field in particular does real work. A client can decide how to render or process a resource, as plain text, as an image, as structured JSON, purely from this field, without needing to inspect the content itself first or guess based on a file extension buried in the URI.
11. Who Decides What Counts as a Resource
The server author decides. Nothing about MCP forces a particular piece of data to be modeled as a resource versus, say, being returned as the result of a tool call.

A well designed server exposes something as a resource specifically when the natural use case is browsing and reading, and reserves tools for anything that represents an action or a computation with inputs.
Modeling this well is a design skill, not a protocol requirement, and getting it right makes a server dramatically easier for a client to use well.

A useful test when designing a server is to imagine explaining the capability out loud to a colleague. If the sentence naturally starts with "let me show you," it is probably a resource. If it naturally starts with "let me go do," it is probably a tool. This small framing exercise catches most modeling mistakes before they ever reach a client.
12. Resources vs Prompts

blocks.alt: A resource supplies data while a prompt supplies instructions
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737276-724235771.png
It is easy to conflate resources with prompts since both feel like they are supplying content rather than doing something, but they answer different questions.

" A resource might be a specific log file, a prompt might be a template for asking a model to analyze any log file handed to it. Resources are covered in this module, prompts get an entire module of their own later.

A useful shorthand: a resource answers "what," a tool answers "do what," and a prompt answers "how should I ask." Keeping these three questions separate in your head makes reading any MCP server's capability list far easier, since you can sort each entry into one bucket almost instantly.
13. The resources Capability

blocks.alt: A server declares the resources capability before a client can see any resources
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737516-106852797.png

A server that wants to expose resources at all declares this during the initialize handshake by including a resources capability in its response. A client should never assume a server supports resources just because most servers do, it checks the capability first, and only sends resources/list or resources/read calls if that capability was actually present.

The subscribe and listChanged flags hint at two more advanced behaviors, being notified when a specific resource's content changes, and being notified when the overall list of available resources changes. Both get their own detailed treatment later in this module.

It is worth contrasting this with tools, which advertise their own capability separately. A server can support tools without supporting resources, or the reverse, or both, or neither. Nothing about MCP requires a server to offer every category of capability, a server that is purely a calculator, for instance, might expose tools only and skip resources entirely since it has no readable state worth exposing.
14. Why the Read vs Do Split Matters for Safety
The entire reason MCP bothers to separate resources from tools this cleanly is risk management.
An autonomous agent wiring together dozens of MCP servers is a genuinely risky thing to build if every capability looks the same to the system deciding what to call automatically.

Because resources are guaranteed to be read only, a host can safely auto-fetch them to enrich context without a human in the loop, while reserving explicit confirmation for anything that could actually change the world.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: If you ever find yourself designing a resource that has a side effect, stop, that operation almost certainly wants to be a tool instead. The safety guarantees the rest of this module relies on assume resources never mutate anything.

blocks.text: This same split is also what makes automated testing and auditing of MCP integrations tractable. A test suite can safely call every resources/read exposed by a server in a loop with no side effects to clean up afterward, while a tools/call test suite has to be far more careful about setup and teardown, since each call might really change something.
15. Where Resources Show Up in a Real Session

In a typical session, resources show up in three moments. First, during capability negotiation, where the client learns resources are supported at all. Second, during discovery, where the client calls resources/list to see what is on offer.
Third, during actual use, where the client, often on behalf of the user or the model, calls resources/read to pull specific content into the conversation.
The next several lessons walk through each of these moments in detail, starting with how a resource gets its identity in the first place.

blocks.text: 16. A Quick Mental Model

If tools are the verbs of MCP, resources are the nouns. A tool is something you do, a resource is something you have. When you are trying to decide, while reading any MCP server's documentation, whether a given capability is a resource or a tool, ask yourself whether using it reads like "give me the current state of X" or "make X happen." That single question resolves the overwhelming majority of cases correctly.
17. Resources Are Not Free

blocks.alt: Reading a resource consumes context tokens
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737519-623258023.png

Even though reading a resource never changes server state, it is not without cost to the conversation itself. Every resource pulled into context consumes tokens from the model's limited context window, so a host application still has to be selective about which resources it fetches and includes, rather than treating "read only" as a license to include everything available. Being safe to fetch is not the same thing as being free to fetch.

blocks.title: Design tip
blocks.content: Good hosts fetch resource metadata for browsing, and only pull full content in when it is actually relevant to what the user asked, keeping the context window focused rather than flooded.

blocks.text: 18. A Note on Naming

Server authors should give resources names and descriptions a human would immediately understand, not internal identifiers or code names. A resource named "Q3 Revenue Summary" with a clear description is far more useful to a client browsing a list than one named "res_00417," even though both might resolve to the exact same underlying data. Since resource discovery often happens without a human reading raw JSON, thoughtful naming is a real part of building a good MCP server.
Worked Example

Imagine a small MCP server built for a support team, wrapping their ticketing system. It exposes two things: a resource for reading a specific ticket by its ticket number, and a tool for closing a ticket.

A host application answering the question "what does ticket 4021 say" would call resources/read on the ticket's URI, get back the ticket's text, and hand that straight to the model, no confirmation needed since nothing changed.

If the user then says "go ahead and close it," the host instead invokes the close_ticket tool, and because that is a tool, most host applications would show the user a confirmation before actually executing it.

The same underlying ticketing system supports both operations, but the server author deliberately modeled reading and closing very differently, and that difference is exactly what lets the host treat them with different levels of caution.
Common Mistakes

items: Modeling an action, such as marking something as read or incrementing a view counter, as a resource just because fetching it also happens to be involved.
Assuming every server exposes resources without checking the resources capability from the initialize response first.

Treating a resource's content as guaranteed to be small, some resources, such as an entire log file or a large document, can be substantial and may need to be summarized rather than dumped whole into a limited context window.
Confusing a resource with a prompt because both feel like they supply content rather than perform an action.
Forgetting that a resource can be dynamically generated, and assuming its content will be identical every time it is read.
Designing a server where reading a resource has a hidden side effect, which breaks the safety assumptions clients rely on.

blocks.text: Practice

Pick any application you use regularly, an email client, a project tracker, a note taking app, and list five pieces of information inside it that could naturally become MCP resources, and two actions that should stay as tools instead. For each resource, sketch what its URI might look like.

code.content:
// Example answers for a project tracker
resource: task://project-42/task-1189       // read a task's details
resource: project://project-42/summary       // read a project's overview
tool:     create_task                        // creates a new task, a mutation
tool:     assign_task                        // changes assignment, a mutation

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

A resource is context you can read, nothing more and nothing less. It is identified by a URI, described by simple metadata, and guaranteed never to change anything when you fetch it, which is exactly what lets a client treat reading resources as low risk compared to invoking tools. Files, database records, documents and configuration are the everyday examples, but the underlying idea generalizes to anything a server wants to let a client observe.

The next lesson looks closely at the one thing every resource must have, its URI, covering how these identifiers are structured, what schemes look like in practice, and the conventions that make a good URI scheme easy for clients to work with.
